concept.body: Classify a coordinate quadrilateral in layers. BASE: parallelogram if both opposite slope pairs match, or (faster) if the two diagonal midpoints coincide. UPGRADES: rhombus if all four squared sides are equal; rectangle if the squared diagonals are equal (or adjacent slopes multiply to −1); square if both. Report the most specific name the numbers support.

explanationVariants: Coinciding diagonal midpoints certify a parallelogram.

widget.prompt: Quadrilateral (0,0), (5,1), (4,6), (−1,5). Its diagonal midpoints both equal (2, 3). What's certified?

options.label: Parallelogram — diagonals bisecting each other is a complete test
options.feedback: pq's diagonal test, executed by the midpoint formula: one computation, base layer done.

options.label: Rectangle
options.feedback: Bisection alone stops at parallelogram — a rectangle would additionally need equal diagonal lengths.

options.label: Just a quadrilateral
options.feedback: Coinciding diagonal midpoints is one of pq's PROVEN parallelogram tests — the certificate counts.

options.label: Square
options.feedback: The square needs equal sides AND right angles on top — midpoint coincidence only buys the parallelogram layer.

steps.body: Four vertices, same discipline — and the quadrilateral course's tests become CHECKLISTS. Parallelogram: both slope pairs match (or diagonal midpoints coincide). Upgrade to **rectangle**: adjacent slopes multiply to −1 (or diagonals congruent). Upgrade to **rhombus**: all four sides equal (or diagonals perpendicular). Both upgrades at once: **square**.

explanationVariants: Slope PQ = 1/5 and slope SR = 1/5; slope QR = 4 and slope PS = 4 — both pairs parallel.
Two matched slope pairs certify the parallelogram.

widget.prompt: P(1, 2), Q(6, 3), R(7, 7), S(2, 6). The slope audit (PQ, QR, RS, SP) finds:

options.label: Both opposite-side pairs are parallel
options.feedback: Both opposite pairs match: the definition itself is satisfied, straight from chapter 2's parallel criterion.

options.label: Exactly one opposite-side pair is parallel
options.feedback: BOTH pairs match: 1/5 = 1/5 and 4/1 = 4/1. The second pair is easy to miss on the steep sides — parallelogram.

options.label: Two adjacent sides are perpendicular
options.feedback: (1/5)(4) = 4/5 ≠ −1 — no right angles here. Just the two parallel pairs: parallelogram.

explanationVariants: Sides: PQ² = 26, QR² = 17 — unequal, so not a rhombus. Diagonals: PR² = 61, QS² = 25 — unequal, so not a rectangle.
Both upgrade tests fail: it stays a plain parallelogram.

widget.prompt: Same PQRS. Checking upgrades — rhombus (equal sides) and rectangle (equal diagonals):

options.label: Neither test passes: parallelogram only
options.feedback: The pq course's most-specific-name discipline, now with receipts: both upgrade certificates fail, the base one stands.

options.label: Only the rectangle test passes
options.feedback: Looks don't testify; diagonals do: √61 ≠ 5. Not a rectangle — parallelogram only.

options.label: Both upgrade tests pass: square
options.feedback: A square needs BOTH upgrades; this figure earns neither. Parallelogram.

explanationVariants: All four squared sides: 25, 25, 25, 25. Diagonal slopes: 4/8 = 1/2 and 4/(−2) = −2 — product −1.
Equal sides say rhombus; perpendicular diagonals co-sign (pq's rhombus signature).

widget.prompt: Quadrilateral (0, 0), (5, 0), (8, 4), (3, 4) — all four sides square to 25. Compute the product of the two DIAGONAL slopes.

commonErrors.feedback: 1 drops a sign — the diagonals run (0,0)→(8,4) at 1/2 and (5,0)→(3,4) at −2: product −1, perpendicular — the rhombus signature.
−0.25 = (1/2)(−1/2) reuses the first slope's reciprocal — the second diagonal's slope is 4/(3−5) = −2: product −1.
0 would need a horizontal diagonal — (0,0)→(8,4) climbs at 1/2. Product: (1/2)(−2) = −1.

widget.fallbackFeedback: (1/2)(−2) = −1 — perpendicular diagonals, exactly what pq promised a rhombus.

predict.prompt: All four sides of this shape will measure exactly 5. Is that enough to make it a SQUARE?

options.label: Yes — four equal sides settle it
Not yet — the corners (or diagonals) still have to be checked
It can never be a square on a slanted grid

predict.reveal: Equal sides make a rhombus. Whether it is also a square is decided by one more check — right angles, or equivalently equal diagonals — and that check is exactly what the shape's own name will report.

widget.prompt: Three corners sit at (0, 0), (5, 0), (8, 4). Place S so all four sides are equal — then read what the shape calls itself.
widget.successFeedback: Four sides of 5 — and the name reads rhombus, not square. Run the deciding check: the diagonals measure √80 and √20. Unequal diagonals mean the corners are not right angles, so equal sides alone never promote a rhombus to a square.
widget.sideFeedback: Track the side lengths: from (8, 4), the fourth corner must sit a distance of 5 from both (8, 4) and (0, 0). Slide across until the two remaining sides match the first pair.
widget.angleFeedback: The across position is right — now the height. The fourth side closes back to (0, 0), and only one height makes both remaining sides equal 5.

widget.prompt: Quadrilateral (0, 0), (3, 4), (−1, 7), (−4, 3): all sides square to 25. Compute the product of two ADJACENT side slopes.

commonErrors.feedback: 1 drops the sign — slopes 4/3 and (7−4)/(−1−3) = −3/4 multiply to −1: right angle, so with equal sides this is a SQUARE.
0.5625 = (3/4)² squares a reciprocal — the adjacent slopes are 4/3 and −3/4: product −1.

widget.fallbackFeedback: (4/3)(−3/4) = −1 — equal sides + right angle = square, fully certified.

hints: Run the layers in order: parallelogram first (slopes or diagonal midpoints).
Then the upgrades: side lengths for rhombus, diagonal lengths (or adjacent slopes) for rectangle.
explanationVariants: Midpoints (3, 4) and (3, 4) coincide: parallelogram. Sides: 58, 26, 58, 26 — not a rhombus. Diagonals: 100 and 68 — not a rectangle. Verdict: parallelogram, and the diagonal-midpoint test did the base work in one line.
Diagonal midpoints coincide at (3, 4); upgrades both fail (58 ≠ 26; 100 ≠ 68). Parallelogram.

widget.prompt: W(0, 0), X(7, 3), Y(6, 8), Z(−1, 5). Most specific name, with the fastest base certificate?

options.label: Parallelogram by matching diagonal midpoints
options.feedback: One midpoint computation certifies the base layer (pq's bisecting-diagonals test); the failed upgrades pin the most specific name.

options.label: Rectangle by matching diagonal midpoints
options.feedback: Bisection is the PARALLELOGRAM certificate — rectangles need congruent diagonals, and 100 ≠ 68.

options.label: Rhombus by matching diagonal midpoints
options.feedback: Crossing at the shared midpoint says parallelogram; rhombus needs equal sides, and 58 ≠ 26.

options.label: Kite by matching diagonal midpoints
options.feedback: A kite pairs CONSECUTIVE equal sides without the parallelogram structure — this figure has coinciding diagonal midpoints: parallelogram.

takeaways: Base layer: parallelogram by slope pairs OR coinciding diagonal midpoints (usually fastest).
Upgrades: equal sides ⇒ rhombus; equal diagonals or a −1 slope product ⇒ rectangle; both ⇒ square.
Always the most specific name — with the computations as receipts.
steps.teaser: Finale of the chapter: proofs that work for EVERY figure at once — variables in the coordinates.
